newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn to decide before year-end on share profit tax.
newsitem.headline: Bonn to decide before year-end on share profit tax.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday he had no plans yet to extend tax on share capital gains and said the government will come to a decision on the controversial tax in the next four weeks.

"I have no plans yet to extend the tax on share capital gains, but at the next meeting of the commission on tax reform we will meet with representatives from the Bundesbank and the bourse to discuss the matter," Waigel said.
Speaking at the launch of the Deutsche Telekom share flotation, Waigel told journalists: "We will take this opinions on board and make a decision this year."
Pressed further on the matter, Waigel quipped: "You will not be able to tickle any opinions out of me that would damage the financial markets."
Werner Seifert, management board chairman of the German bourse operating company Deutsche Boerse, said he strongly opposed the introduction of a tax on share gains.
"This will just drive capital out of the share market," Seifert said.
Waigel's comments echoed those of the state secretary at the department of Finance, Juergen Stark, who said a decision this year was imminent.

As the tax law currently stands, there is no tax on share gains if investors do not cash in shares within a six-month speculation period. Recent rumours in the market have expressed fears that the speculation period will be extended to one year.

For example, investors who bought shares in Monday's Telekom public offering who cash in their shares on the first day are liable to income tax, which can be up to 53 percent in Germany. This does not apply if the share gains are under 1,000 marks.
Government tax experts said that if the legislation is changed, it will not affect those shareholders who invested prior to the new law.

The proposal to introduce capital gains tax, as part of an overall programme of tax reform in Germany, was proposed in a policy document from the Christian Democrat party, which is the partner party of Waigels CSU in the ruling coalition.
Waigel is chairman of the commission on tax reform in Germany, which aims to lower Germany's overall tax burden. Bonn plans to introduce the new programme in 1999.
